HOUSE of Delegates,

You are assembled to deliberate upon the affairs
of this Commonwealth, and as many questions of
importance have arisen among the people, you will
be called upon to give to them your earnest attention
and profound regard.

The wishes, desires and most important interests
of our constituents are intimately known, and have
been confided to YOU in the strongest hope to animate
them all that the attention and perseverance, ne-
cessary to their accomplishment will not be want-
ing on your part.

In a country like ours, spread over vast ex-
tent of territory, combining variety of soil, CLIMATE
and productions, and a consequent variety of mi-
nterests, it ceases not to be a matter of surprise, it oc-
casionally the smooth course of legislation should be in-
terrupted by apparent inequalities in its progress,
as difficulties present themselves in many forms, and
in none more injurious to the welfare of the coun-
try than supposed collision of interest in the va-
rious and distinct parts of the Commonwealth;
nor is it unfortunately found to be true, if viewed in
the spirit of the Constitution, mutual concession and
tolerance, than this imaginary conflict of int-
erest presents, in fact no insurmountable barrier to
the attainment of results equally beneficial in all.

To remove the prejudices of some, and alleviate the
discontent of others and to harmonize the competing
interests, as far as is practicable, is duty the
statesman owes to his country, an effort which
none can neglect to make without incurring a
serious responsibility, not only to the present GENE-
ration, but to posterity.

The obstacles removed and union restored to
our councils, the field opens before you on which
you may enter with full assurance of success, pos-
sessing of ample means within your reach and the ne-
cessary power over those subjects, the ACCOMPLISH-
ment of which will render our country strong,
powerful and prosperous, and will bind our citi-
zens by the strong ties to the integrity of the

State.

Among the most important of these objects may
be deemed that of uniting the most distant regions
of the State by means of Rail Roads and Canals,
thereby attending to an easy, safe and rapid
conveyance of the products of our industry to the
best markets.

It is hoped that those
national works which have already been projected,
would meet with your fostering care, and by a
timely appropriation of the funds within your
reach, would advance to successful completion.
Were they already in operation to receive the in-
creased and increasing products of the Agricul-
ture, the revenue arising from them in a few years
would be more than sufficient to meet all ordinary

on the other hand in any GREAT emergency, as in
the case of war, or any other public danger, when the
country would be called upon for increased disburse-
ments and increased velocity of movement, the
very great advantages arising from such state
of things, must be taken to all should
we then at any future DAY be involved in war.
An assessment of taxation, exacting from the people a
sum no greater in amount than is now required
would perhaps be equal to our wants and would
hardly be felt.

The line of improvement deemed most impor-
tant to the State, and the only one which, without
vast disbursements, will ever be found capable of
connecting the Atlantic with the great West, is that,
which is contemplated by the James and Lower Ka-
nawha rivers. The Commonwealth has heretofore
retained the property in those rivers; but at the last
session an act was passed, authorizing certain
sum of money to be subscribed by indivi-
duals by which they would become joint stock-
holders with the State in this great work ACCORDING
to their respective interests invested.

failed. Should individuals not have subscribed the
amount required, no alternative would be left us
but to resume and prosecute the work to its full
completion, in style that will make it as prof-
itable to the State as its singular advantages
leave no room to doubt.

Organized militia is of such vital impor-
tance to the defence of free people, so indispens-
able to the preservation and protection of their LIB-
erty, that I must again present this subject to your
early and serious attention. In vain may we
hope for safety and long security unless we have
the means of making ourselves felt and respected.

guishing from the thriftless and unproductive
character of slave labor. I cannot speak in
detail on the operations of agriculture, but I
can refer you to interesting results as exhibit-
ted by the tabular records of our exports.
The population of the states north of Mason
and Dixon's line, is 18,676,693 souls. The
population of the states south of that line, is
7,258,714 souls. During the year 1829, the
domestic exports north of this line, amounted
in value to $34,961,907, and the like exports
south of it amounted to $37,396,764. From
which it appears that the products of the re-
spective divisions were about in the ratio of
their population. Again, the population of
the United States is 11,935,404 souls. The
population of Virginia, Georgia, Alabama,
North and South Carolina—which are the
chief slave holding states, is 3,556,910 souls,
or about one fourth of the whole. The do-
mestic exports of the United States in 1827,
amounted in value to $558,921,691. The do-
mestic products exported from the five states
above mentioned, during the same period, am-
ounted to $158,574,953, or about one third
of the exports of the Union—with a popula-
tion to one third. Again, the population of Penn-
sylvania is 1,147,673 souls; of Virginia is
1,211,272 souls. The domestic products
exported from the former in 1827, amounted
to $80,189,296, while those from the latter a-
mounted to $4,646,137. What do these re-
sults prove but that the production of the
slave states is greater, in proportion to popu-
lation, than that of the non slave holding
states? And such is doubtless the fact. The
people of this State, white and black, labor
as advantageously, and produce as much, as
any equal number of whites, elsewhere.
Why then is Virginia poor and in debt? Not
sir, because she has nothing for market, but
because she is defrauded in the sale of her
produce and the purchase of her supplies
from abroad. The course which commerce
has taken, from causes which it is neces-
sary here to examine, is disastrous, in the ex-
treme, to Virginia, as well as the other south-
ern states. During the year 1829, the im-
portations to the north of Mason and Dix-
on's line amounted to $560,001,501, while
those to the south of it were only $14,450,566—
and yet the products exported from
the latter division during the same period, as
already stated, exceeded those from the for-
mer, by nearly three millions of dollars.
Here lies the greatest of all our misfortunes.
The northern states import all the goods and
we of the south buy our supplies from them.
They act both as merchants and carriers,
and in that combined character, engross the
whole commercial profit. It is this annual
tribute to the north, superadded to enormous
duties on imports, that keeps the south poor;
and it is this same tribute which makes the
north rich and builds up those splendid man-
sions and cities of whom we have heard so
much in this debate.
